The DIY process for mead making is extremely simple. The initial materials I used:

  • Bleach. Used in highly distilled amounts to clean all equipment. Don't use dishsoap to clean equipment, dish soap might gel up somewhere inside equipment and cause a bad ferment.

  • Glass 1 gallon carboy bottles. (I used glass to ensure no bacteria would get in seams as they might with plastic bottles). Have at least two per the type of mead you're making. The second bottle is used for the secondary fermentation.

  • Hand siphon

  • Lalvin Dried Wine yeast #EC-1118

  • Honey. The less filtered the better. I used some bulk stuff from Costco, but if you can get less filtered honey in bulk, more power to you.

  • Raisins. A small handful are used in each batch to help the yeast along.

  • Brewing airlock. One per carboy.

  • Optional: Fruits. I used frozen blackberries, frozen strawberries, and fresh oranges. The frozen berries were heated in the microwave and chopped, the orange was simply chopped. They were all added to their respective carboy batches. You can experiment how you want or use existing recipes out there.

  • Old wine bottles

  • Corks and a hand corker from a wine store.

Procedure:

  • I cleaned everything with a tiny bit of bleach and a lot of water.

  • Heat up a small amount of water until it is slightly warm and let the yeast sit in it. This was to "wake up" the yeast and make it more effective.

  • Heated the honey slightly in a pan on the stovetop.

  • Added 2 pounds of honey to about 1/2 gallon of water. Shook the mixture vigorously.

  • Added the yeast, optional fruit, and 4-5 raisens. Again shook everything vigorously.

  • Cleaned the top of the carboy with a towel and installed the airlock.

After this I put the carboys in a dark slightly warm spot. Within the day they were obviously foaming and reacting. I let them sit for about a month when all of the yeast bubbling had completely stopped. I gently took the carboy out and used the hand siphon to take the liquid from the old carboys into fresh ones, leaving behind a bottom layer of scummy sediment. I left the mead to ferment in the second carboy for 3 more months. Then siphoned it into wine bottles and corked them.

Super easy, just takes patience and care not to contaminate the batches during handling.
